WEDNESDAY, 13 OCTOBER 2010 
Mr Speaker took the Chair at 2 p.m. 
Prayers. 
MOTIONS 
Burma—Human Rights 
Hon MARYAN STREET (Labour): I seek leave to move a motion without notice 
and without debate relating to freedom of expression and assembly in Burma. 
Mr SPEAKER: Is there any objection to that course of action being followed? There 
is no objection. 
Hon MARYAN STREET: I move, That the House call on the Burmese authorities 
to guarantee the three freedoms of expression, association and peaceful assembly, and 
call for the immediate and unconditional release of all political prisoners arrested for 
their peaceful opposition to the regime. 
Motion agreed to. 
QUESTIONS FOR ORAL ANSWER 
QUESTIONS TO MINISTERS 
South Canterbury Finance—Recapitalisation Offer 
1. Hon DAVID CUNLIFFE (Labour—New Lynn) to the Minister of Finance: 
What was the net present value at Crown cost of capital of any offer presented to the 
Crown in respect of the recapitalisation of South Canterbury Finance, either on or 
following 31 August 2010? 
Hon BILL ENGLISH (Minister of Finance): I first congratulate the member on 
getting to question No. 1 so soon. I do not intend to comment on commercial details of 
bids or transactions that may be still under negotiation. I refer the member to my 
ministerial statement of 8 September 2010, which addressed this issue. I repeat that no 
option was available that did not involve considerable cost and risk to the Crown. 
Treasury was in close contact with all the parties involved at the time, and no option put 
to us was recommended by Treasury. We accepted Treasury’s advice. 
Hon David Cunliffe: I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker. The Minister has 
essentially declined to answer the substantive question on, I believe, public policy 
grounds, but I seek to clarify through you, Mr Speaker, whether he is invoking the 
public policy ground for not releasing any further information about the net present 
value of those offers. 
Mr SPEAKER: I take it that the Minister is declining to provide the specific 
information asked for because he believes it is not in the public interest to do so. I think 
he has made that fairly clear. 
Hon David Cunliffe: Using the Crown cost of capital, what was the net present 
value of the offer presented to the receiver on 31 August 2010, of which the receiver 
said in a memorandum to staff on 3 September: “After careful consideration and 
consultation with the appropriate parties, including both the trustee and the Treasury, 
this offer was not accepted.”? 
Hon BILL ENGLISH: I could not be exactly sure which offer the member is talking 
about. There has been quite a bit of speculation in the public arena about offers that may 
or may not have been made. Some of the speculation I have seen is clearly wrong, and 
some of it may just be from bidders who felt that Treasury or the receiver should have 
accepted their bid but did not. 
14408 Questions for Oral Answer 13 Oct 2010 
Hon David Cunliffe: I seek leave to table the memorandum to all staff from the 
receivers, Kerryn Downey and William Black of McGrathNicol, dated 3 September 
2010, which notes consultation with Treasury and that the offer made in respect of 
South Canterbury Finance was not accepted. 
Mr SPEAKER: Leave is sought to table that document. Is there any objection? 
Hon Simon Power: He should do it at the end. 
Mr SPEAKER: No, the member has sought leave to table it. I take it that there is no 
objection? There is no objection. 
Document, by leave, laid on the Table of the House. 
Hon David Cunliffe: I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker. As the receivers’ 
memorandum makes it clear that the offer presented on that date, 31 August, was not 
accepted, I submit to you that there can be no commercial confidentiality ground around 
that offer that would prevent the Minister from answering the primary question and the 
subsequent supplementary question. 
Hon Simon Power: It’s a debatable point. 
Mr SPEAKER: The Minister should not be interjecting. The member raises an 
interesting issue. The dilemma for the Speaker is that the Speaker cannot judge whether 
divulging information is or is not in the public interest. On this occasion the Minister 
has made it pretty clear that, in his view, to say any more about these particular matters 
is not in the public interest. I have to take the Minister’s judgment on that. The member 
can question the Minister about that through further supplementary questions, but I 
cannot tell a Minister that he or she is wrong if the Minister believes that it is not in the 
public interest to divulge something.  
Hon David Cunliffe: Further to the point of order, Mr Speaker, I totally respect your 
judgment on that matter, but I draw your attention to the fact that the Minister used a 
specific rationale for declining to answer the primary question in the public interest, and 
that was commercial confidentiality around an ongoing matter. It is clear from the 
document that has been tabled that it is not an ongoing matter, at least in respect of the 
offer of 31 August, because that offer has been rejected already by the receivers. I guess 
it stands for the Minister then either to specify a new public policy ground or to answer 
the primary question. 
Mr SPEAKER: I have to stress that the public interest is a matter for the Minister to 
judge, not for the Speaker. Given the answer the Minister has given, I believe that the 
member can challenge the Minister with further supplementary questions on why he has 
that view.  
Hon David Cunliffe: What advice did he receive from Treasury in respect of the 
offer for recapitalisation of South Canterbury Finance dated 31 August, and what 
response did he or his colleagues make to that advice? 
Hon BILL ENGLISH: As I have said, I do not intend to speculate on any particular 
offer. The member is referring to one dated 31 August. There was any amount of 
discussion going on around that time that some people may have thought consisted of 
making offers and some did not think were offers. The fact is that the Government now 
has the obligation to recover the value of those assets, and it is certainly our intention to 
preserve the commercial processes around that. It simply will not work if anyone who 
makes some kind of offer to the Crown finds that that offer is discussed in detail in 
Parliament, when it was made in the context of commercial confidentiality. It may be 
that the offer he is referring to came from people who are bidding again as we speak, 
because the Government is open to offers all the time for the assets of South Canterbury 
Finance. It is not a matter of trying to be evasive; it is just a matter of trying to preserve 
a process that is designed to get maximum value for the taxpayer. We do not want to 
13 Oct 2010 Questions for Oral Answer 14409 
scare away bidders as a result of the fact that we are willing to discuss their offers at any 
time in the public arena. 
Hon David Cunliffe: I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker. In noting that the Minister 
has declined to answer the substantive question, which asked what advice he had 
received and what his response was, I note that that advice pertained to a past offer that 
has already been rejected. Further, it is my understanding that the parties involved are 
not currently in negotiation for the assets of that company, as the Minister may have 
alluded to. I cannot see—and perhaps you may clarify this with the Minister—what the 
public interest ground is upon which he is refusing to answer the question. 
Mr SPEAKER: On these matters the Speaker has to be guided by the Minister. The 
issue of public interest is a matter for the Minister. As Speaker I cannot judge that. I 
should not judge that, and I must not try to. Where it is a matter of public interest not to 
divulge certain information, and where the Minister is alleging that is the case, those are 
important matters. I must not interfere in that. I think that is a very important, 
fundamental issue, especially where it has commercial implications. As the Minister has 
pointed out, even though the member might be referring to a past offer, it does not mean 
to say the party involved may not be still involved in negotiations. So I have to be 
guided by the Minister on an issue like that.  
Chris Tremain: What steps is the Government taking to ensure that the workings of 
the Crown Retail Deposit Guarantee Scheme are fully transparent?  
Mr SPEAKER: Well, I suppose the deposit guarantee scheme was the reason why 
the Crown had—I shall allow the question, even though it is a fair stretch from the 
primary question. 
Hon BILL ENGLISH: Clearly some parts of the process will occur without total 
transparency. For instance, if bidders are making offers and they are turned down, or if 
they want to change those bids or come back again later in the process, the Crown wants 
to make sure that opportunity is available. However, it is appropriate that, given the 
amount of public funds spent on this scheme, it is independently scrutinised. That is 
why yesterday I welcomed the news that the Auditor-General will complete a 
performance audit of the deposit guarantee scheme. In addition, this week Treasury will 
make an initial release of over 100 documents relating to the scheme, including 
documents relating to South Canterbury Finance’s participation in it. That will 
demonstrate that the Government and officials have worked towards our objectives of 
providing depositors with certainty, and minimising the costs to taxpayers and 
disruption to the economy.  
Hon David Cunliffe: What was the net present value, at Crown cost of capital, of the 
revised offer presented to the receivers on 13 September 2010 by Kensington Swan on 
behalf of Permanent Investments Ltd, and acknowledged in a letter from the receiver 
dated 14 September; and can the Minister confirm that the potential participants in that 
recapitalisation included the New Zealand Superannuation Fund and Ngāi Tahu?  
Hon BILL ENGLISH: It is not my role to confirm or otherwise any of the details of 
that matter. That would be up to those organisations. I stress to the member that it is 
vital the Government recovers as much as it can of the $1.6 billion that it is in the 
process of paying out. We intend to conduct a process whereby Treasury is overseeing 
and working alongside the receivers to ensure we get the maximum value for those 
assets. Regular parliamentary discussion and speculation about who made which bids is 
the role of the Opposition, but it is not a game that the Government will get into, 
because it will destroy value and prevent us from recouping as much of that $1.6 billion 
as we can.  
Hon David Cunliffe: Can the Minister confirm that Ministers did provide guidance 
or advice to officials on those offers, given that he was quoted in the Dominion Post on 
14410 Questions for Oral Answer 13 Oct 2010 
1 September saying that he would be “a close adviser” to the receivers, and that the 
Prime Minister was quoted in the Dominion Post on 1 September saying that the 
Government had assumed sole rights in respect of South Canterbury Finance because 
“without that we would be in the position of being the 800-pound gorilla who would 
have to take marching orders from a mouse.”? 
Hon BILL ENGLISH: The Government has been running a process where it takes 
advice from Treasury. Prior to the receivers being in place, that advice from Treasury 
would have been based on information coming from the company itself, and after the 
receivers were in place on information that came from the receivers. I might say, 
though, that the business of whether there were offers around at that time has been 
subject to a lot of speculation. I will repeat to the member that some of that speculation, 
from what I have seen, is simply wrong. Otherwise, the Government does not intend to 
get into discussing the details of offers, and in many cases we would not have been fully 
aware of all the dimensions of those offers. 
Hon David Cunliffe: I seek leave to table a printout of a Dominion Post article dated 
1 September that verified the quotations that I have just used. 
Mr SPEAKER: We are not going to seek leave to table recent press releases. 
Hon David Cunliffe: I raise a point of order Mr Speaker. We have got ourselves into 
an interesting situation. I submit to you that the Minister has quoted public interest 
grounds for refusing to provide any substantive answers whatever to the Opposition’s 
questions on this matter. Mr Speaker, I further submit that that is inappropriate, because 
the evidence suggests that the Government has deliberately—as verified by those 
quotations—left hundreds of millions of dollars of taxpayer money— 
Mr SPEAKER: No, no. The member will resume his seat. The member is now 
starting to argue the substance of the matter. The reason why I am not putting leave to 
the House to table a clipping from a newspaper is that the member has already referred 
to the quotes in his question. Anyone can look them up in the newspaper; we are not 
going to waste the time of the House by tabling clippings from recent newspaper 
articles. 
Hon David Cunliffe: If Ministers had decided to accept another outcome from the 
receivership than that presented in the office on 31 August or 13 September, can the 
Minister confirm whether this alternative outcome will have a greater or lesser net 
present value than the $1.3 billion contained in the offer of 31 August? 
Hon BILL ENGLISH: The Government is taking the steps that it believes are 
required to maximise the value of the sale of the assets. With South Canterbury Finance 
having gone into receivership, the Government said at the time it was not interested in a 
fire sale, and we do not believe that a considered and value-creating process should be 
knocked over by an aggrieved bidder. If the member has an aggrieved bidder who 
thinks that he or she missed out, well, that is interesting. I am sure that he will get more 
of them, because in the end there will be people who try to buy these assets cheaply 
from the Government, where the Government does not agree to sell the assets to them. 
Hon David Cunliffe: If there were considerations other than protecting taxpayer 
value—which the Prime Minister set out as the Government’s primary objective—that 
informed this Minister’s decision not to accept either of the offers of 31 August and 13 
September, what were those considerations, and why did they outweigh the 
Government’s goal of protecting taxpayer funds, when it would appear from documents 
that up to half a billion dollars of taxpayers’ money has been wasted by this secretive 
and mismanaged bail-out?  
Hon BILL ENGLISH: All I would say to that member is that I am sure he will find, 
as his experience increases, that aggrieved bidders will try to use political means— 
13 Oct 2010 Questions for Oral Answer 14411 
Hon David Cunliffe: I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker. Given that it is the 
Minister who appears to have wasted half a billion dollars on this matter— 
Mr SPEAKER: Order! 
Hon David Cunliffe: —how about he answers the question— 
Mr SPEAKER: When I get to my feet the member will resume his seat 
immediately, if he wishes to stay in the House. The member asked a question in which 
he made an assertion towards the end of it about the amount of money he claimed the 
Government had wasted. The Minister, faced with a question like that, will have a fair 
bit of licence in answering it.  
Hon BILL ENGLISH: As the member becomes more experienced in these matters, 
I think he will realise that aggrieved bidders—if that is what he has—are not necessarily 
the most reliable sources of information or judgment on whether they should have got 
the assets. I am sure that having raised the matter in this way, he will attract further 
aggrieved bidders who do not meet our objectives. 
Dr Russel Norman: Will he rule out the sale of South Canterbury Finance’s land 
assets to overseas buyers? 
Hon BILL ENGLISH: Well, I cannot rule that out, simply because that would be a 
show of bad faith, given that we have an Overseas Investment Act in place. The 
member will be familiar with the changes that the Government has announced to that 
Act, which will be in place by 1 December, and anyone who seeks to buy those land 
assets would have to follow that process. For the House’s information, South 
Canterbury Finance is a one-third shareholder in the land assets, and it would be 
possible for the holders of the other share in those assets to perhaps buy South 
Canterbury’s. But that is yet to be seen.  
Economy—Reports 
2. JOHN HAYES (National—Wairarapa) to the Minister of Finance: What 
recent reports has he received on the economy? 
Hon BILL ENGLISH (Minister of Finance): I have received reports showing that 
the economy is in better shape than it was 2 years ago. The economy has grown for five 
consecutive quarters, following an extended recession that began in early 2008, well 
before the global financial crisis. The 1.7 percent economic growth in the last 9 months 
exceeds the 1 percent growth posted over the entire 4 years up to the beginning of 2010. 
I have also seen reports that households and businesses are moving away from 
excessive spending and borrowing, which were features of our lopsided economy in the 
past decade. Instead, they are paying down debt and being careful with their spending. 
This change is welcome, but it is happening faster than we expected. 
John Hayes: What roles is the Government’s tax package playing in helping to 
rebalance the economy? 
Hon BILL ENGLISH: The economy needs to rebalance from an excessive reliance 
on Government spending on borrowing and housing, towards exports and investment 
and savings. That is what the tax package is designed to do, to push in the direction that 
people are already going. The increase in GST will discourage excessive consumption, 
the increase in the effective tax rate on property will in effect discourage speculative 
investment in property, and the reduction in income tax reduces the tax on savings, jobs, 
exports, and investment. 
Hon David Cunliffe: Has he received reports that the price of fruit and vegetables 
has gone up, and although the increase of 2.6 percent in September may be down to 
winter, the further price increases since then are all because of National’s increase in 
GST, inflicting greater costs on hard-working Kiwis who are struggling to make ends 
meet? 
14412 Questions for Oral Answer 13 Oct 2010 
Hon BILL ENGLISH: The member may care to take note of the Governor of the 
Reserve Bank’s comments from the annual report yesterday. He said that the inflation 
risk from GST is, as he describes it, muted so far. 
Hon David Cunliffe: That’s only because the economy is collapsing. 
Hon BILL ENGLISH: Well, it is a very competitive market out there and retailers 
have to be careful about putting their prices up. However, people are guaranteed to get 
their income tax cut. When they look at their after-tax pay over the next few weeks, they 
will realise just how far $4 billion of income tax goes. In respect of vegetables—and 
there are 17 of them in the Labour caucus—in the 2 years to September 2008 they went 
up 21 percent under Labour. In the 2 years to September 2010 they went down 6 
percent. 
John Hayes: What other contributions is the Government making to helping New 
Zealanders through this adjustment and setting the economy on a faster growth path? 
Hon BILL ENGLISH: I think the most significant contribution the Government is 
making is to absorb the shock of this recession on the Government’s books. This fiscal 
year the Government will run a cash deficit of $13 billion—that is, the Government is 
borrowing $13 billion over the next 12 months to continue with an infrastructure 
investment programme to maintain transfers and to ensure that Government services 
remain in place at a time of stress. This is supporting New Zealanders through the 
adjustment process, but it cannot last for ever and the Government will have to tighten 
up on its spending in order to bring those deficits back to a surplus. 
John Hayes: What economic policies would damage New Zealand’s economic 
prospects and leave the vast majority of Kiwis worse off? 
Hon BILL ENGLISH: The policies that will do that are policies that create more 
borrowing, larger deficits, more Government debt, and higher cost of living increases. 
They are also policies that repeat the mistakes of the last Labour Government when it 
reduced the incentive to work and to save and to invest. I understand that Labour will be 
announcing details of policies going in that direction this week— 
Hon Darren Hughes: I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker. I have been listening to 
the answer the Minister is giving. He is not responsible for policies that are being 
developed by the Opposition, no matter how frightened he might be by them. 
Mr SPEAKER: The member is quite right that the last part of the answer was really 
out of order; fortunately it was mercifully brief. But the member was absolutely right 
with his point of order. 
Marine and Coastal Area (Takutai Moana) Bill—Access Under Customary Title 
3. Hon SHANE JONES (Labour) to the Attorney-General: Does he agree with 
ACT leader Rodney Hide’s statement on Radio New Zealand this morning in relation to 
ACT’s amendment to the Marine and Coastal Area (Takutai Moana) Bill to explicitly 
prohibit Māori with customary title from charging fees for access to coastal areas: “I

Hon RODNEY HIDE (Leader—ACT): I move, That the House take note of 
miscellaneous business. I am very proud that the ACT Party is the only party in this 
House that has had the same position on the foreshore and seabed legislation from day 
one, while every other political party has flip-flopped from one side to the other. The 
ACT Party has stuck to its principles, and the principles are these: to stand up for New 
Zealanders’ property rights, to stand up for the rule of law, and to stand up for one law 
for all. That is why we opposed the Labour Government’s move to torpedo iwi and 
hapū rights to have their day in court. That legislation was wrong, and the ACT Party 
opposed it. Iwi, like all New Zealanders, should be able to have their day in court. What 
Labour did was a travesty. 
When National and the Māori Party came to see the ACT Party about what should be 
done, the ACT Party’s view was simple; it was to repeal the Foreshore and Seabed Act, 
to use Parliament to return iwi and Māori to their position pre-2004 that allowed iwi and 
Māori to go the High Court, and to legislate for free public access. That was ACT’s 
position in 2004; that is ACT’s position in 2010. That is ACT’s position now, and it is a 
principled position on the rule of law. 
We thought the foreshore and seabed legislation was a shocker; the Marine and 
Coastal Area (Takutai Moana) Bill is far, far worse. It defines an entirely new set of 
statute-made property rights. It sets up a process that enables the New Zealand 
coastline, our foreshore and seabed, to be carved up and privatised across iwi hands, so 
that not only do they own the foreshore and seabed but they control its use because they 
become the consenting authority. No other New Zealander can do that; that is wrong. 
Iwi should be able to go to court and seek customary title, and not have Parliament 
define what that customary title is. 
But it is far worse than that, because the foreshore and seabed legislation enables iwi 
to go and see the Attorney-General and negotiate a settlement, rather than go to court— 
Dr Paul Hutchison: Do a deal! 
Hon RODNEY HIDE: Dr Hutchison is absolutely right. Iwi are able to do a deal 
behind closed doors to say: “Hang on, how much do you think we should own of the 
foreshore and seabed?”. The Attorney-General is on record as saying that National 
thinks it should be about 10 percent, which is about 2,000 kilometres of coastline. So 
according to the Attorney-General, iwi would own 2,000 kilometres of coastline. How 
did the Attorney-General come to that figure? How did the Attorney-General hold it to 
2,000 kilometres? What mandate does any Government have—does this Parliament 
have—to establish ownership rights in the foreshore and seabed, and have those rights 
granted, politically, in a Minister’s office? ACT says “None!”. That is divisive, it is 
discriminatory, and it is against the rule of law. It is against one law for all. The only 
principled position for this Parliament to adopt is to say that of course iwi, Māori— 
Hon Clayton Cosgrove: Oh, oh—principled? You couldn’t spell “principled”. 
Hon RODNEY HIDE: —even Clayton Cosgrove—can have their day in court. 
The Court of Appeal decision was plain. The court said that of course iwi could have 
their day in court, but it did not think they would succeed because it is tough to prove 
customary title. The Government is saying not to worry about that; the Government will 
drop the threshold so that Māori can meet it. The Government can hand across the 
coastline and no one even needs to go to court. They can just pop into Chris Finlayson’s 
office and he can sign on the dotted line. That is wrong.

Hon ANNETTE KING (Deputy Leader—Labour): Before I begin today, I would 
like to acknowledge Mr Jim Currie, who was a messenger in this House for 5 years in 
the 1980s—a man whom I know that you also know, Mr Speaker. I went to his funeral

gentleman and a much-loved member of many sporting clubs in my electorate, and I 
pass on the sympathies of this House to Mr Currie’s family. 
What I will talk about today is: what is leadership? That question has been 
dominating the debate over the airways and in the pages of our publications and on the 
blogosphere over the past 2 weeks. That debate has been triggered by the Prime 
Minister’s response to the racist and inappropriate remarks made by the so-called shock 
jock Paul Henry. Questions have been raised, such as, when should a Prime Minister 
show leadership? Is political leadership applied only in certain circumstances? Is 
political leadership available only from 9 until 5? Does political leadership not apply 
when one is dealing with one’s mates? Does political leadership require insight? Does it 
require courage, a quickness of thought? Does it require real convictions? 
I believe that these are all legitimate questions when it comes to analysing John 
Key’s giggling deflection of Paul Henry’s comments about the Governor-General—
about his ethnicity, the colour of his skin, his birthplace, and his manner of speech. 
When I listened to John Key’s response that morning, a quote from Albert Einstein 
came to mind. He said that in the case of political leaders, it is often very doubtful 
whether they have done more good or harm. In my view, there is no doubt that the 
Prime Minister’s limp-wristed, giggling, and joking response to the provocative, hurtful, 
and racist comments made by Mr Henry has been harmful. 
Most New Zealanders see their leaders as people who guide and who inspire. People 
like to have leaders who make them feel proud. Leaders are not people who just bask in 
the reflected glory of other people’s achievement, but people who make us, as Kiwis, 
feel that we have something to contribute in securing a better world and a future for us 
all—like leading the fight against nuclear weapons; standing up against discrimination 
of women, disabled people, and people of different sexual orientation or ethnicity; 
fighting against apartheid; or refusing to join the Iraq war because it was not sanctioned 
by the international community, even though considerable pressure was applied by our 
friends. Real leadership requires taking a stand, having a genuine belief in one’s 
policies, and standing up for those beliefs. Genuinely held beliefs are not tradable 
commodities at an election to secure votes, nor are they tradable commodities during an 
interview on television to retain friendship, to look matey, or—to quote John Key—“to 
be cool”. 
I believe that John Key failed the test of leadership during the Paul Henry interview. 
His instinct was to pander to Paul Henry, not to slap him down for his racist comment. 
His moral compass was missing. Where was his belief and conviction against racism? 
Eight hours after the furore had reached a crescendo, the Prime Minister issued a very, 
very weak press release. I have yet to hear the Prime Minister make a speech that sets 
out what his genuine beliefs are, what his bottom-line convictions are, and the issues 
that would make him take a stand, come hell or high water. What I have heard from the 
Prime Minister are the utterances of a person used to taking a gamble on other people’s 
futures—short term, expedient, here today and gone tomorrow, and increasingly to 
smile and walk away. 
Winston Churchill once said “There is no worse mistake in public leadership than to 
hold out false hopes soon to be swept away.” In my view, John Key campaigned on 
false hopes. I think people are starting to see him as the emperor with no clothes and 
they are noticing his nakedness.

Dr RUSSEL NORMAN (Co-Leader—Green): I start today by congratulating 
Mayor elect Celia Wade-Brown. The counting of the special votes has been finalised 
today, and Celia Wade-Brown has been elected mayor of our capital city, Wellington. It 
is an interesting development that both Wellington and Auckland—congratulations also 
go to Len Brown in Auckland—are led by mayors who support sustainable transport 
options. We now have the bizarre spectacle where the Minister of Transport is 
completely at odds with the leadership of two of the largest cities in our country, 
Auckland and Wellington— 
Sue Moroney: And Hamilton. 
Dr RUSSEL NORMAN: —and Hamilton as well. Pro-train councillors have been 
elected in Hamilton.  
A spectre is haunting the Minister of Transport, and that spectre is green transport 
options. For the first time we find that leaders of our major urban centres are promoting 
sustainable transport options, while the Minister of Transport is locked in the 1950s 
with his idea that we can build motorways to reduce congestion. Building motorways 
does not reduce congestion; building motorways induces more traffic and results in 
more congestion. As Transit used to say famously, all we ever do is move the 
congestion point.  
There is one really good way to reduce congestion in our major urban centres. The 
people who have just voted in the local body elections in Auckland, Wellington, 
Hamilton, and elsewhere have chosen that particular method, and that is mass public 
transport. It is also active transport such as cycling and walking. When we build trains 
and train lines, when we build light rail, when we have more efficient bus services, and 
when more people can walk or cycle to work, then we reduce the amount of traffic on 
roads. It is one of the paradoxes that the major beneficiaries of more public transport are 
road users, because it frees up the roading network when more people move off the 
roads and into mass transit or active transport options.  
The other side, of course, is that it reduces our greenhouse emissions and makes our 
cities much more livable. New Zealand has very high transport greenhouse emissions. 
They have increased by about 70 percent since 1990, and that is connected to our 
obsession over the previous 10 years with building more and more motorways and 
inducing more and more traffic, and hence consuming more and more oil. It is also tied 
to the fact that oil is a finite resource. Just today the Parliamentary Library released a 
paper that looked at some of the issues around oil. The paper concluded that oil was 
going to increase in price quite significantly. It looked at international projections as 
well as domestic projections, and the impact that increase would have on our domestic 
transport options. Of course, our domestic transport system is entirely dependent on oil 
because we have thrown billions and billions of dollars at white elephant motorway 
projects, instead of into sustainable transport options that actually reduce oil use.  
If we wanted to get home faster, then we would support the kinds of options that 
people in Wellington and Hamilton have just voted for, such as better public transport. 
If we wanted to reduce our greenhouse emissions, we would support those options. If 
14432 General Debate 13 Oct 2010 
we wanted to reduce our dependence on oil, we would support those kinds of 
sustainable transport options. If we wanted to live in more sustainable and more livable 
cities, where we do not have giant motorways slicing and dicing our communities, then 
we would support those kinds of sustainable transport options. That is exactly what the 
people of Auckland, Wellington, and elsewhere have just done.  
We now have the bizarre situation of conflict with central government, which is still 
dominated by people from the 1950s who think the solution to congestion is to build 
more motorways. We have the conflict between the 1950s thinking of Steven Joyce and 
the National Government, and what the people of Auckland and Wellington are 
desperately calling out for. They are the ones who live in big urban centres and 
understand that we cannot reduce congestion by building more and more motorways. 
That does not solve congestion. The urgent priorities in Wellington are around light rail, 
both to the airport and to the hospital. The urgent priorities in Auckland are around a 
train system that extends through the central business district loop and also out to the 
airport.  
This is a great day for green politics in New Zealand. It is a great day for everyone 
who supports sustainable transport options for Aotearoa New Zealand. 
MICHAEL WOODHOUSE (National): The 2010 barbecue season appears to have 
started early, perhaps as early as 28 July. Recent revelations about our friends on the 
other side remind me of the ditty from that great Gilbert and Sullivan opera The 
Mikado. Instead of the Lord High Executioner, we have the “Lord High Executed”, and 
instead of Ko-Ko of Titipu, we have “Carter of Te Atatū” and he has a little list. After 
Catherine Delahunty’s maiden speech I vowed I would never sing in this House, but if I 
did, the song could go something like this: “As some day it may happen that a leader 
must be downed; he’s got a little list. Seventeen offenders who really must be found; 
he’s got a little list.” I certainly agree that none of them would be missed, but I am sure 
Mr Goff would certainly love to get his hands on it.  
When Mr Carter finally does leave this place, and I do not think it will be long, he 
might want to consider a new career as a game show host. Remember Jason Gunn’s The 
Rich List? Well, Mr Carter could front a new show called “The Ditch List”. Labour MPs 
could appear and attempt to name as many of their colleagues as they can who are ready 
to roll their leader. That would be one show where getting a good score might be a bit 
career limiting. What is most astounding about this whole affair is that Mr Carter has 
been very indiscreet; in fact, he was so clumsy in his attempt to undermine his leader 
that I suspect that that was his intention all along. He is probably very upset that his 17 
colleagues did not follow him into the coup d’état after he led them out of the trenches.  
The most astounding point about this is that Mr Carter’s main criticism is absolutely 
accurate in respect of the extraordinary flip-flop on GST. Mr Carter rightly points out 
how inconsistent the Labour leader, Phil Goff, is being when he dusts off the big red 
bus, paints the words “Axe the Tax” on the side of it, and crusades around the country 
telling people how badly off they will be. 
But when it comes to the crunch, he cannot commit to axing the tax—quite the 
opposite. He now commits to keeping the rate of GST, but tinkers around the edges of it 
with fruit and vegetables. After 25 years of Labour defending the efficiency of GST—
25 years, including Dr Cullen deriding any suggestion of differential rates of GST—in a 
desperate move, he proposes to tinker with the policy. If Mr Goff really has a problem 
with the tax switch and if Labour genuinely believes New Zealanders would be better 
off by returning GST to 12.5 percent and handing back the $4 billion of tax cuts they 
just received, then he should take that policy to the electorate at the next election.  
Labour members repeatedly state that those changes do not favour the many but 
favour the few, so they should have the courage to go to the electorate and wind back 
13 Oct 2010 General Debate 14433 
those changes. They should tell a family on the average income who has just got $25 a 
week more in its pay packet despite the GST switch that Labour wants to take that back 
off them. Labour members should tell the married superannuitants who receive a 
minimum of $12 more a week, and whose income under this Government has gone up 
by over $100 a fortnight, that they want to return this country to the tax-and-spend 
policies that led New Zealand into the brittle economic state this Government found 
itself in. Those members should have the courage to go back to the electorate and turn 
the policy into action. I suspect that that was what upset Mr Carter and the 17 members 
sitting on the other side of the House the most—talking big, but not following through.  
Who might be on the list of 17? Well, one could probably discount the most recent 
arrivals to Parliament, so that takes down the suspect list to about 28. If we take away 
the leader and the deputy leader, we are left with 26. If we take away those who have 
retired or announced that they are not standing at the next election, because they are 
bound to be ambivalent about the leadership, that is another four or five, so we are now 
down to about 21 possible Labour members. That is 21 Labour members who did not 
come in at the last election, who still plan to be around after the next election, and who 
are not the leadership pair. Seventeen of them are very possibly on Mr Carter’s list. So 
17 of the 21 more experienced members who want to stick around next year could be 
exposed by Mr Carter as wanting to roll their leader. The aspirants to leadership know 
that timing is everything. They would probably be happy to let Mr Goff fall on his 
sword after the next election, but they might be thinking about moving sooner now on 
the basis that if they do not, someone else might. On the other hand, what will it mean 
to be exposed by Mr Carter as a member of the list of 17? Well, it probably augurs 
pretty well for their plans. That will be of comfort to the aspirants as the barbecue 
season approaches. 
Hon CLAYTON COSGROVE (Labour—Waimakariri): If Mr Paul Henry did 
not know, or did not have examples of, what it means to be a New Zealander then there 
is something wrong with him, given that in my view and in the view of certainly most 
people in this House there are 4.2 million examples in this country of what it means to 
be a New Zealander, what it sounds like to be a New Zealander, and what it looks like 
to be a New Zealander, and they are called our community.  
I say that because as Annette King said, we have not only in the last couple of weeks 
but in the last month seen two key and critical failures of leadership on behalf of the 
Prime Minister. The first was to not defend the Governor-General. That was a failure, 
not just simply because he is the Governor-General but—and I suspect there would not 
be a member of this House who would not agree with me in saying this—because he 
represents of himself and his good lady wife, Lady Susan, the essence of New Zealand: 
a decent human being, a decent Kiwi, and a decent person. That was the first strike. The 
second strike, which was some weeks before, was to not hold a Minister in his 
Government, Rodney Hide, to a high standard that he himself promoted as early as 
November 2008 when he said: “I expect high standards from my Ministers. If they don’t 
meet the standards I set, then obviously I will take action if necessary.”  
What were the series of excuses that the Prime Minister used to not stand up, to not 
show leadership, and to not reflect the feeling in the community, which was one of 
anger, emotion, and revulsion in respect of Mr Henry? The first excuse was, to quote 
him, he was “jetlagged”. The second excuse was to say: “Well, you know Paul. You 
never know where he’s going.” The third excuse was that the Prime Minister said: 
“Where there’s freedom of speech, there is always those who will push the boundaries.”  
I say to the Prime Minister that he also has a thing called freedom of speech. He also 
has that great principle that we hold dear, called freedom of speech, but he chose not to 
use it. He zipped his lips and he used the fourth excuse, which was to blame Television 
14434 General Debate 13 Oct 2010 
New Zealand, 3 days later. He used his freedom of speech, which he countenanced in 
Paul Henry, 3 days later. 
I say to the Prime Minister that it was not Rick Ellis, the chief executive of 
Television New Zealand, sitting on the couch with Mr Henry, being interviewed, and it 
was not any of the executive team of Television New Zealand sitting on the couch with 
Paul Henry, being interviewed, so why does he blame them? Oh, no, that was an alibi as 
the giggle, the smile, and the wave occurred. It was in fact the Prime Minister sitting on 
the couch with his best mate and former Tory candidate Paul Henry. The Prime Minister 
showed no fortitude in articulating the emotion of New Zealanders, in using his freedom 
of speech to rebuke Paul Henry, to utterly reject what he was saying, and to defend a 
symbol and a person who is a decent New Zealander. He giggled, he waved, and he 
chose not to use his freedom of speech. He used the excuse of jetlag, and then he 
blamed Rick Ellis and Television New Zealand. Well, I say again that it was not Mr 
Ellis sitting on the couch, being interviewed, who had the opportunity to rebuke Paul 
Henry. It was not Mr Ellis or his executive team who were elected Prime Minister of 
this land and have a responsibility to show leadership.  
I say to Government members that although they squawk and giggle, and poke a bit 
of fun at Mr Carter, at our expense—one can see the likeness of that coming through—
there is a big issue. That issue is about freedom of speech, it is about leadership, it is 
about articulating the hurts and concerns of New Zealanders, and it is about showing 
some guts; it is about showing some guts.  
In that respect I turn to the Hide fiasco. Mr Hide talked today about high principle. I 
could not believe my luck when Mr Hide talked about the Foreshore and Seabed Act 
and deals done behind closed doors. If there was ever a person who has been 
inconsistent on every principle that he has stood for, whether it be perks, David Garrett, 
zero tolerance, or name suppression, it is that member. Mr Hide could not spell the 
word principle. He did the ultimate deal behind closed doors, aided and abetted by 
Garth McVicar, who knew about David Garrett. He was aided and abetted, he knew 
about it, but he did nothing. Where is the principle in that? I say that that is the other 
failure of Mr Key, as Mr Hide hangs like a millstone around his neck. Where is the high 
standard he promoted in 2008, and where is Mr Key showing leadership in holding that 
Minister to account? He has zero points on Paul Henry and zero points on Mr Hide. 
NIKKI KAYE (National—Auckland Central): Today there is a tale of two parties. 
We have a party on the other side of the Chamber that is sinking. It is actually quite sad 
to watch that. What we can see—and it is a pretty standard tactic when we see a ship 
sinking—is the tactic of diversion. That is exactly what we have seen today from 
Annette King and Clayton Cosgrove. They have chosen to divert the whole argument to 
one about our Prime Minister, but here are the facts. The facts are that Labour MPs have 
been jumping ship from that caucus for a long period of time. We have seen Dr Cullen 
go, Winnie Laban is nearly gone, and we will see George Hawkins go.  
But the one person who is staying is Chris Carter. He is sticking around, because he 
is going to spill the beans. That is right. What he is talking about is what I am calling 
the “Save Labour 17”. I can hear right now some people clicking away and creating a 
Facebook page called “Save Labour 17”. I can tell members that—and we have done 
the numbers here; we have done the numbers—when we start to look at the number of 
MPs who would be in that list, we see the fact is— 
Hon Trevor Mallard: I wouldn’t go down here if I were you, Nikki Kaye. 
NIKKI KAYE: That member has the numbers; he has the numbers. Anyway, the 
reality is that there are not 17 members but 18 members on that list, because one of 
them is munching a bagel in New York as we speak. There are actually 18 members on

13 Oct 2010 General Debate 14435 
We see a party that is in absolute disarray. I could not believe it when Annette King 
stood up today and asked what leadership was. I will tell that member that she asked 
exactly the question that is being asked in the offices of all her party’s MPs right at the 
moment. The irony was incredible. The irony was incredible when she chose to give a

to ask that question out loud, what is going on in the Labour Party? That was actually a

That situation contrasts with what this Government is doing, so I will tell Annette

where we have real front-line public services. Leadership is about making changes to 
the Resource Management Act, so that thousands of New Zealanders do not have to 
spend time and money on bureaucratic processes. Leadership is saying it is not fair in 
this country to allow one in five kids to leave school without being able to read and 
write. We see a Government that is making real change to New Zealand in terms of 
education, the economy, health, and the environment, compared with a party that, sadly, 
is completely imploding. 
Dr CAM CALDER (National): I noticed the Hon Chris Carter was due to speak 
next, but he does not appear to be in the House. 
The ASSISTANT SPEAKER (Eric Roy): The member cannot refer to the absence 
of another member. That is a caution. 
Dr CAM CALDER: “A plan” was the braying chorus we heard from those on the 
benches opposite as the collective caucus uni-neurone briefly glowed from time to time. 
A question we may well ask is whether they would recognise one. Would they 
recognise a plan? Why do I suggest that? It is because for an interminable period in 
Government they appeared to operate without one. As a result, year after year after year 
in times of unparalleled global prosperity the performance of our tradables sector 
dropped ever further behind. Slumped in their armchairs of apathy and indolence, 
dressed in pyjamas in the daytime, feet encased in the woolly slippers of indecision and 
hesitation, a rug of torpor on their knees, wearing nightcaps of incomprehension and 
bemused incompetence, what plan did they espouse when they had their arthritic, 
twisted talons on the levers of power? What plan was there?  
Long-suffering New Zealanders were taxed, regulated, and subsidised. Small-
business men and women, as well as exporters, were effectively told to stand by, to 
hurry up, and to wait. Labour had no plan; its position instead appeared to be that if 
something moved, tax it; if it continued moving, regulate it; and if it stopped moving, 
subsidise it. Innovation, creativity, and entrepreneurship were stifled; a fresh idea was 
as rare as a Bantu at a bar mitzvah, and the tradables sector wilted. Its default position 
of supervised neglect meant that our economy underperformed despite the best 
economic conditions since Noah took a day off to go fishing.  
Most New Zealanders were blithely unaware of the previous administration’s 
mismanagement as the calamitous state of affairs was masked by ever more overseas 
borrowing and ill-directed spending. As the global recession approached, little changed; 
no one in the home for the bewildered noticed. The background muffled whiffling and 
cackling continued unbroken save for the odd curse or oath as one resident tried to 
snatch another’s bauble of office.  
14436 General Debate 13 Oct 2010 
That continues to this day. Coups are plotted, denied, discovered, and the rank and 
file of the Labour caucus look on bemused as senior members squabble in the sand pit. 
Instruction in party policy and doctrine are solicited and received from union leaders on 
the outside. Senior members are draped in sackcloth and ashes, ritually humiliated and 
excommunicated from the party; they leave muttering dark threats and imprecations.  
We are told of a long list of Labour caucus members unhappy with their leader. Who 
could be on that list? Potentially, almost every second member of the Labour caucus. 
New Zealanders are asking the question: “If this is Labour’s level of self-government, 
how could it ever be fit to run the country?”. The economic mess the previous Labour 
Government left behind proved that it was not fit to run the country and Labour 
members’ current antics also show they are not fit. All that is missing is the death rattle.  
John Key’s principled, pragmatic National-led Government has set out a plan to deal 
with the worst recession in seven decades and has reshaped the economic mesh in many 
areas and at different levels. We are focusing relentlessly on lifting New Zealand’s 
long-term economic growth to create jobs, boost incomes, and raise the living standards 
of the hard-working people of Manurewa, where I am privileged to be based, and, 
indeed, of all New Zealanders. 
Our society is judged by how we treat our most vulnerable. We need to grow the 
economic cake in order to provide the world-class public services that all New 
Zealanders deserve. To paraphrase Lao-tzu a bad Government is despised, a good 
Government is revered, a great Government, the people say they did it themselves. This 
National-led Government is aspirational for our country. We are working hard to 
provide families in our communities with the financial security, the opportunities, and 
the higher incomes they need to help unlock the potential within each of them to pursue 
their individual dreams and aspirations and create a brighter future for themselves. Our 
1 October tax package is rewarding effort. It will help attract and retain skilled people in 
New Zealand and help hard-working families to get ahead. Thank you. 
BRENDON BURNS (Labour—Christchurch Central): The last couple of 
National speakers have chosen to touch on issues of leadership. If members opposite 
want to talk about leadership by the Prime Minister, I ask where he showed leadership 
when our distinguished Governor-General was being slagged on a breakfast television 
programme and racist and offensive remarks were made right in front of him. Where 
was leadership shown by him in not responding to those questions on the spot? John 
Key is one of three people who bear responsibility for this very unfortunate saga—one 
of the three. Paul Henry has paid the price for the comments he made, and appropriately 
so, but John Key and the chief executive of Television New Zealand (TVNZ) bear 
responsibility, as well. 
We have to say that the Prime Minister failed to recognise and stand up for the 
interests of the 100,000 New Zealanders of Indian origin when Paul Henry made his 
racist and offensive remarks about a person of Indian descent not being an appropriate 
choice as the Governor-General. I wonder whether this weekend the Prime Minister will 
attend one of the many Diwali events around the country as our Hindu community 
celebrates its sacred festival. Will he stand shoulder to shoulder alongside members of 
the Indian community and enjoy their hospitality, when he failed so miserably recently 
to defend their interests, to defend the reputation of a man who grew up in that 
community, who has been a distinguished New Zealander, and who, in front of an 
audience of hundreds of thousands, was denigrated on our State television channel?  
I think John Key bears as much responsibility for that as Paul Henry. Not only did he 
fail to challenge those racist and offensive remarks, but also he sat there for the next few 
minutes and virtually encouraged Paul Henry to continue. Paul Henry continued his 
offensive comments. He then started questioning who should be the next Governor-
13 Oct 2010 General Debate 14437 
General, and the Prime Minister allowed him and encouraged him to rule out two other 
distinguished New Zealanders: one a former member of this House, Jeannette 
Fitzsimons, and the other the Mad Butcher, Sir Peter Leitch, whom, ironically, Paul 
Henry was due to host on This Is Your Life last weekend. The Prime Minister sat there 
like a stuffed dummy and allowed not just one distinguished New Zealander but three 
distinguished New Zealanders to be denigrated. I say that is an issue of leadership. 
When a remark like that is said in front of politicians of any stature, certainly at Prime 
Minister level, politicians need to find their moral compass and stand up and say it is 
unacceptable and it is offensive. It deserves to be responded to immediately; they 
should not sit there, smile, and wave. The Prime Minister failed a large section of the 
New Zealand community at a time when it wanted true leadership. 
It is not the first time that Paul Henry has caused offence, and, in fact, that is where 
the question mark about the judgment of TVNZ and its chief executive comes into 
question. I note that there has been a series of events like this one that have been 
increasingly trenchant and have increasingly caused division and offence in the 
community. Until now there has not been any attempt by TVNZ to rein in that 
presenter. It sat by and said publicly that he was a bit naughty but, by golly, he rated! 
That should not be the only requirement of a State-owned broadcaster. We should have 
expectations that a State broadcaster will have some requirement other than simply to 
maximise ratings and revenue. That is why it is the State broadcaster. It is a shame on 
TVNZ.  
I acknowledge that Paul Henry has been on air through two Governments, but 
members should note that, as one media commentator put it, he seemed to go really 
ballistic from the time of the change of Government onwards. Part of the reason for that, 
of course, is that this Government has told TVNZ to ditch any other requirement; to not 
think about issues of national identity, balance, ethics, and judgment, but simply to 
focus on the bottom line and to maximise the dividends for this Government. When that 
kind of requirement is put on TVNZ, this sort of thing is no surprise. That said, we 
expect people in positions of authority, like the chief executive of TVNZ, who is also 
editor-in-chief, to recognise the commercial risks he is putting upon his company.  
I think the real motivation for TVNZ’s taking action against Paul Henry at the level it 
has done was not really the response of hundreds and hundreds of New Zealanders—the 
biggest ever response—but the threat of one of its major advertisers to pull its 
advertising. That is what rang TVNZ’s bells. That is what caused it to intervene and 
respond, not the fact that tens of thousands of New Zealanders were personally offended 
by the comments made in the presence of the Prime Minister, who failed to defend the 
integrity of our Governor-General. Shame on him. 
Dr JACKIE BLUE (National): I am truly delighted to take part in this general 
debate. This month is October, Breast Cancer Action Month. Yesterday I hosted a Rural 
Women New Zealand initiative called Let’s Get Plastered for Breast Cancer. Not 
surprisingly, the title of the event captured everyone’s attention. Getting plastered was 
not about getting rolling drunk, but rather about women and some men taking plaster 
casts of their chests and displaying them anonymously, with the proceeds going to 
breast cancer. This was quite a fun event, enjoyed by many, but there was a very serious 
message behind it. Getting plastered is about promoting breast cancer awareness, which 
is an important tool for all women of all age groups. It is important that women 
understand the normal breast changes, and particularly changes in their breasts that 
persist. We are very fortunate to have a high-quality breast-screening programme—
BreastScreen Aotearoa, known as BSA for short—which targets women between the 
ages of 45 and 69, when the most benefit is seen. But we know mammograms are not 
perfect, and there are cancers that appear between mammograms and, indeed, outside 
14438 General Debate 13 Oct 2010 
the screening age. That is why it is important that women get to know what their normal 
breast tissue is like, and, when changes persist, act to see their doctor.  
Very importantly, the Let’s Get Plastered event was about raising money for the New 
Zealand Breast Cancer Foundation. I acknowledge the vital work that the foundation 
does in breast cancer education and awareness. The fact is that this country needs a 
vibrant charitable and voluntary sector; without it, quite frankly, many of our support 
and social services would be next to impossible. So my congratulations go to the 
foundation for the work it does.  
Breast cancer is the most common cancer for New Zealand women, and one of the 
leading causes of cancer-related death. Each year, approximately 2,600 women are 
diagnosed with this cancer, with more than 650 dying of this disease each year. The 
Government is committed to improving the numbers of people affected by breast 
cancer, as well as the survival rates. It is pleasing to know that the proportion of New 
Zealand women accessing BreastScreen Aotearoa continues to increase, and it is 
particularly heartening to see that coverage rates for Māori and Pacific Island women, 
where generally coverage is lower, and survival statistics are poorer compared with 
other women, are increasing. That is a positive step in the right direction.  
There has also been good progress in breast reconstruction. For many women who 
have a mastectomy and choose to have their breast reconstructed, it is definitely not a 
cosmetic procedure; it is a vital part of their treatment and their healing. In 2006 Hutt 
Valley District Health Board decided it was unable to offer delayed breast 
reconstruction to women of the central and Nelson-Marlborough regions, due to 
resource constraints. In April this year the Government announced in the Budget that $8 
million over 4 years will go to the Hutt Valley District Health Board to deal with the 
backlog of women from the central and Nelson-Marlborough regions. This will allow 
100 women to get secondary breast reconstructions this year, which is tremendous news 
for those women. 
Chris Auchinvole: It certainly is. 
Dr JACKIE BLUE: Absolutely. The Government has sent a clear message also that 
reducing cancer treatment waiting-times is one of our top priorities. This is reflected by 
the fact that radiation oncology times are now covered by one of the Government’s six 
key health targets. Under the National Government not one woman has had to be sent to 
Australia for radiation treatment, and that is just fantastic—not one woman. District 
health boards are now aiming for every person needing radiation treatment to receive it 
within 4 weeks; that will be a target by December this year. That is an astonishing

13 Oct 2010 Governor-General Bill 14439 
GOVERNOR-GENERAL BILL 
Second Reading 
Hon CHRISTOPHER FINLAYSON (Attorney-General) on behalf of the Prime 
Minister: I move, That the Governor-General Bill be now read a second time. As the 
Prime Minister indicated when the bill received its first reading, it is very important and 
timely legislation. It was referred to the Government Administration Committee on 20 
July; the committee has now completed its examination of the bill and has 
recommended that it be passed. 
The bill implements the Law Commission’s recommendations in the first part of its 
review of the Civil List Act 1979. This bill will repeal and replace Part 1 of the Civil 
List Act with updated financial arrangements for the support of the office of Governor-
General. The new regime will be more transparent and simpler to administer, and it will 
also modernise the antiquated drafting of the Governor-General part of the Civil List 
Act. 
The bill contains a comprehensive transitional regime. With one exception, the new 
legislation will not apply to the incumbent. Clauses 25 and 27 contain savings and 
validation clauses to ensure the relevant provisions of the Civil List Act and any 
determinations of the Remuneration Authority or Orders in Council made under that 
Act relating to salary, payments on leaving office, and other benefits or privileges 
continue to apply to the incumbent and to previous Governors-General and their 
spouses. Only the annuities provisions, which remove certain outdated restrictions on 
the availability of the annuity, will apply to the incumbent and to his spouse. 
The core of the bill is directed to reforming the financial support structure of the 
office of Governor-General. The present regime is, as the Law Commission recognised, 
cumbersome and unclear. Funding for the Governor-General is split between two sets of 
appropriations, one funding the official residences and part of the Governor-General’s 
programme of activities, and the other paying for the Governor-General’s salary and 
allowance, but also including aspects of the Governor-General’s programme. The bill 
addresses this issue by consolidating all funding for the Governor-General’s programme 
within a single permanent appropriation, leaving annual appropriations to account only 
for the Government House operational budget. To provide further transparency, the bill 
will also separate out funding for the Governor-General’s international travel from the 
appropriation providing for the Governor-General’s domestic programme. 
Unlike the domestic travel programme, which the Governor-General determines 
himself or herself, international travel is undertaken at the request of the Government. 
Because this travel is often difficult to predict in advance—for example, requests to 
attend significant funerals—the Government has agreed with the Law Commission’s 
recommendation that a new permanent appropriation be established for this purpose. 
A key feature of the bill is that it will remove the exemption from income tax on the 
Governor-General’s salary. Both the salary and the allowance are presently exempt 
from income tax under the Income Tax Act 2007, and the salary is calculated on that 
basis. As noted by the Prime Minister, there is no longer any justification for this salary 
to be exempt from income tax. Her Majesty the Queen has voluntarily paid income tax 
on her private income since 1993 and the Australian Governor-General and state 
governors have paid income tax on their salaries since 2001. 
A further tax-related change is the removal of the Minister of Finance’s power to 
exempt the Governor-General from paying any public or local tax, duty, rate, levy, or 
fee. There are no current exemptions. The Law Commission recommended that the 
power be removed, and it has not been carried over into this bill. 
14440 Governor-General Bill 13 Oct 2010 
The Government Administration Committee identified one small issue with the bill 
that will need to be addressed in the Committee of the whole House. The Goods and 
Services Tax Act 1985 presently excludes from the definition of “taxable activity” any 
engagement, occupation, or employment pursuant to the Civil List Act 1979. For the 
avoidance of doubt, section 6(3)(c)(i) will need to be amended to read “pursuant to the 
Civil List Act 1979 or the Governor-General Act 2010”. 
Section 3(4) of the Civil List Act provides that on leaving office the Governor-
General shall be paid a sum equal to 3 months’ tax-exempt salary and 3 months’ tax-
exempt allowance. The purpose of this payment is to cover the outgoing administration 
and immediate commitments of the outgoing Governor-General. The Law Commission 
recommended that this payment should be retained, albeit in a new form. Following the 
first reading of the bill, there was a degree of misunderstanding concerning this 
payment, including the suggestion that it would double in size under the new bill and 
that it would apply to the incumbent. That is not correct. Because the legislation will 
subject the Governor-General’s salary to income tax and significantly reduce the 
quantum of the allowance, the quantum of the payment made on leaving office would 
be reduced if the formula from the Civil List Act were carried over to the new bill. So 
the Law Commission has recommended that the formula be reframed to allow for a 
payment of 6 months’ taxable salary only. Once the Remuneration Authority has taken 
into account the effect of income tax on the salary, it is expected to be a rough 
equivalent to the current payment. The payment will be subject to income tax 
administered through the PAYE system, but the change will not apply to the incumbent. 
Section 4 of the Civil List Act provides for the payment of annuities to former 
Governors-General and their spouses or partners. The annuities are treated as taxable 
income. It recognises the contribution the Governor-General and his or her spouse have 
made to the country, and the ongoing commitments that can arise from a Governor-
General’s duties even after leaving office. These commitments often include obligations 
such as patronage of causes that they come to be associated with during their term, 
considerable correspondence, delivering speeches, and attending various events. The 
public nature of the role often places limits on their subsequent activities and their 
employment choices. 
The Law Commission recommended that the Governor-General Bill should provide 
for the payment of an annuity to former Governors-General in similar terms to the 
present section 4 of the Civil List Act as applied by the Remuneration Authority. This 
annuity will be payable from the date that is 6 months after the date on which the person 
ceased to hold office, rather than 3 months as provided for under the Civil List Act. 
Consistent with the Civil List Act, when a former Governor-General dies, the 
surviving spouse or partner of that person will be entitled to annuity at half the yearly 
rate at which the annuity would have been payable to the former Governor-General had 
he or she not died. These entitlements will also apply to the surviving spouse or partner 
of a Governor-General who dies in office. In the case of a surviving spouse or partner, 
the annuity is based on recognition of the significant role played by the spouse in 
supporting the office holder. That being the case, the Law Commission recommended 
that the annuity should not end if the spouse remarries or enters into a new relationship. 
The other exemptions are also anachronistic and they will be removed by the bill. 
This is an important bill that clarifies the position of the office of Governor-General. 
The office is a very important component of our constitutional framework. It is certainly 
one deserving of respect by everyone at all times. I commend the bill to the House.

The Governor-General Bill, in repealing and replacing Part 1 of the Civil List Act, 
could be interpreted as simply being about remuneration, income tax, duties, rates, 
levies, and fees. Indeed, the intention of the bill is to facilitate improved financial 
arrangements for the support of the Governor-General and his or her programme. To

months’ non - tax-exempt salary. This is an amendment that has arisen out of the 
recommendation of the Law Commission, which the Government Administration

concerning the salary allowances and the travelling expenses of the Governor-General. 
The amendments will enable the arrangements to become more transparent and simpler 
to administer, and a key change is that the bill removes the tax exemption status of the 
Governor-General’s salary. From this point on, the Governor-General will pay income 
tax equally with every other New Zealander, ending the Governor-General’s tax-free 
status.

position of the Governor-General, and I will speak to that point, which is so relevant in 
the light of recent events in the public media. The relationship between the position of 
the Governor-General and the constitutional framework of Aotearoa dates back as far as 
1840, to the signing of Te Tiriti o Waitangi, which provides the fundamental context of 
our nationhood. On 6 February 1840 the Treaty of Waitangi was signed by Queen 
Victoria’s representative, Governor William Hobson, and ultimately by some 500 
rangatira Māori. Ever since that time the Governor-General has been an important 
representative of our founding document. He or she represents to every New Zealander

Governor-General Bill as it is also an important means of being able to consolidate the 
relationship between tangata whenua and the Crown, and, in doing so, to promote the 
concept of an enduring nationhood.  
The Governor-General has had a significant presence at some of the most distinctive 
moments in the history of this nation. It was Governor-General Sir Cyril Newall who 
took part in the ceremony at Ruatōria on 6 October 1943 to honour the Māori 
Battalion’s Victoria Cross winner, Second Lieutenant Te Moananui-a-Kiwa Ngārimu, 
an event attended by more than 7,000 Māori from all over New Zealand. It is the 
Governor-General who appoints members to the Waitangi Tribunal to investigate 
claims of breaches of the Treaty from 1975 onwards. It is the Governor-General who 
represents the monarch at the historical Waitangi Day events.  
I share with the House the words of Dame Silvia Cartwright in 2005: “I encourage all 
New Zealanders to support and engage in our uniquely indigenous culture and language.

BILL (NO 2)

House: I move, That the Subordinate Legislation (Confirmation and Validation) Bill

finally to the House by 15 November 2010, and, notwithstanding the Standing Orders, 
13 Oct 2010 Subord. Legislation (Confirmation & Validation) Bill (No 2) 14455 
that the committee can meet on a Friday in a week in which there has been a sitting of 
the House, during a sitting of the House, or during an evening on a day on which there

Sue Moroney: Why are you extending them? 
Hon JOHN CARTER: If members sit and listen, they will be told why the bill 
needs to be put through by that time. The bill confirms or validates items of subordinate 
legislation that must be confirmed or validated by Parliament. This is a requirement of 
the empowering Acts under which the various orders or regulations have been made. 
The role played by the House in confirming or validating the various items—and, in 
particular, the scrutiny provided by the Regulations Review Committee—provides an 
additional layer of protection in the regulation-making process. Should the House 
decide to withhold its approval for a particular regulation or order contained in the bill, 
that regulation or order will lapse. That said, this bill traditionally receives cross-party 
support.  
All of the orders and regulations in this bill are certainly of a technical character. 
There are 15 orders or regulations listed in the bill that are to be confirmed or validated. 
They have been made under 10 different Acts. I shall provide a brief summary for the 
benefit of the House of each instrument confirmed or validated by the bill.  
One set of regulations is made under the Animal Products Act 1999. These 
regulations make a variety of minor changes to animal product - related matters, 
including confirmation of the new fee charged for a reissue of official assurance, of the 
annual registration fee for transport operators, and of the applications to list as a 
certified supplier of pet food, and an increase in the basic hourly charge on certain 
export and game sectors.  
An order made under the Biosecurity Act 1993 allows for the imposition of levies on 
particular goods imported into New Zealand. The order sets out the basis upon which 
the levy is calculated and sets a maximum levy rate of $18 per leviable importation. The 
order also makes some technical changes around the arbitration process for determining 
who is required to pay a levy, and the amount that is payable.  
The bill includes an order under the Civil Aviation Act 1990. The order sets a 
domestic passenger levy that is payable by the particular airline operators. Two 
commodity levies are confirmed. The first is a levy on meat—defined as beef and sheep 
meat—produced by livestock farmers. The second is a levy on New Zealand - grown 
grapes that are used to make wine, grape juice, or grape juice concentrate.

Dr PAUL HUTCHISON (National—Hunua): It gives me pleasure to continue 
speaking on the Human Assisted Reproductive Technology (Storage) Amendment Bill. 
As I was saying, this bill came about after media inquiries to the Minister of Justice. 
There was concern that clinics acting in good faith could be storing embryos and 
gametes—that is, sperm and eggs—illegally. The whole point about this bill is to make 
the rules around storage absolutely clear; that, indeed, has successfully been achieved 
by this legislation. The bill now clarifies the rules around storage. This is very, very 
important because of the hugely emotional area that this bill encompasses, particularly 
for patients, and, of course, because of the very important legal issues for clinics. That 
part of it has been very satisfactory.  
In terms of the various parts of the bill, one of the aspects that people raised their 
eyebrows about a little was the issue of gametes and embryos that are stored in other 
countries. Indeed, it was vital to ensure that we dealt with this area accurately, because 
storage outside New Zealand clearly must be counted as part of the 10-year period. 
International tourism is literally going on with regard to in vitro fertilisation around the 
world; in the order of 10,000 couples a year travel from one country to another. So it is 
particularly important to ensure that the storage rules are very clearly defined.  
There were calls during the debate to provide a review mechanism for the Act, but 
the view was that generally this legislation has worked very well so far, that there have 
been no complaints, and that because it is relatively new legislation and because it 
requires flexibility, it is not appropriate at this stage to consider a review. But it is 
important that we keep that matter in mind in the future.  
One aspect of the debate that stood out was the concerns expressed by the Māori 
Party. Te Ururoa Flavell said in the first reading of the bill: “The Māori Party has a 
considerable sense of sadness that we even have bills like this in front of the House … I 
cannot say that anyone in the Māori Party is at ease with the discussions around assisted 
reproductive technology,”. Further to that, Hone Harawira cemented in those views and 
made known some fairly strong concerns about the technology, and said that Māori 
were being left out. He cited a variety of papers in his speech, which I took the bother of 
13 Oct 2010 Human Assisted Reproductive Tech. (Storage) Amdt Bill 14459 
looking up, and I was quite surprised by them. The first one was by Mārewa Glover and 
Benedicta Rousseau, ‘Your child is your whakapapa’. I found this paper to be very 
convoluted, wordy, full of sociological verbiage, and lacking in any precise conclusion. 
To give members an example, one of the pages in this report is entitled “Strategic 
Naturalizing and the Fluidity of Relatedness”. I found this very hard to understand. It 
says: “It is important to stress here the preliminary nature of the data on which this 
article is based. The majority of the participants involved in hui did not have direct 
experience of AHR, or necessarily infertility. They were a predominantly self-selected 
group of interested people who, through the research process, became ‘informed lay 
people’.”  
What I am concerned about is that the members actually admitted to me that they 
were merely parroting references that they had been given to speak about in their 
written speeches. One of the others cited was Te Tauranga Waka, an action plan for 
addressing Māori concerns about the system and process for the ethical review of issues 
relating to human participation in research and innovative technologies. That was 
slightly more practical in its key actions and recommendations. But the message that I 
would give to the Māori Party is that there is a tremendous amount of thinking behind 
the human-assisted reproductive technology legislation. Philosophers, ethicists, lawyers, 
clinicians, and scientists have for years worked to get this legislation in New Zealand as 
good as it could be. I urge the Māori Party to look at the writings from the Advisory 
Committee on Assisted Reproductive Technology, and from the Ethics Committee on 
Assisted Reproductive Technology, as well. The concerns to ensure that thought is 
given to Māori aspects are right at the forefront. In fact, the Human Assisted 
Reproductive Technology Act requires that everyone exercising powers or performing 
functions under the Act must be guided by its principles, including the principle that the 
needs, values, and beliefs of Māori should be considered and treated with respect. I 
believe there is a reciprocal responsibility for members of the Māori Party to take the 
time to read the very well-considered literature in this area.  
I will end by making mention of the fact that on 4 October the Nobel Prize 
committee awarded to Dr Edwards the Nobel Prize for medicine or physiology. It was, 
of course, in 1978 that the first test-tube baby was born, and since then something like 4 
million babies—the population of New Zealand—have been born through the use of 
these technologies. I think it is important to remind the House just how remarkable 
these technologies can be for people who are affected by infertility. In fact, Professor 
Edwards said that in his view the most important thing in life is having a child. Nothing 
is more special than a child. From my point of view, there is no doubt that for those who 
have trouble conceiving—and it is almost one in five couples—birth technologies are 
amazing and positive, provided they are used with humanity and are used ethically and 
wisely. I believe this amendment bill, which we have been discussing over the last few 
months, is part of New Zealand’s contribution towards ensuring that we clarify the rules 
as much as possible, that we have a strong ethics background to back them up, and that 
our clinics around New Zealand give wise counsel to the many patients who come to 
them.
